title: Skull surgery in the Andes

confidence.note: More than 800 trepanned skulls from Peru have been studied, the oldest dated to about 400 BCE. Survival rates are inferred from healing at the edges of the holes, a sound but indirect method, and why most operations were done is reconstructed from associated injuries rather than written records.

people: John W. Verano, Tulane University bioarchaeologist who studied the Peruvian skulls
David S. Kushner, University of Miami neurologist and co-author of the 2018 survival study
summary: Ancient Peruvians cut holes in living skulls for some 2,000 years, and by Inca times most patients survived.
body: Peru has yielded more trepanned skulls than the rest of the world combined: over 800 of them, from the coast and the Andean highlands, some with as many as seven holes cut or scraped through the bone. The earliest, from Peru's southern coast, date to about 400 BCE. The practice lasted through the Inca empire until the Spanish conquest, and healers in highland Peru and Bolivia were still reported doing it in the twentieth century.

Bone records whether the patient lived. Smooth, remodeled edges mean healing; a raw edge means death during or soon after the operation. Read this way, only about 40 percent of patients survived in 400–200 BCE. Between 1000 and 1400 CE survival reached 91 percent in some samples, and in the Inca period it averaged 75 to 83 percent, as surgeons learned to make smaller openings. Fractures from sling stones and clubs were common in the highlands, and treating head wounds was probably a main purpose.
Cranial surgery in the American Civil War killed 46 to 56 percent of patients. How Andean surgeons controlled pain and infection is unknown; they left no written records.

myth.tradition: Inca surgeons are often said to have numbed their patients with coca leaves or other plant drugs.
myth.record: That is plausible but unproven. The researchers who measured survival rates say no written records exist, so what was used against pain is simply not known.

links.note: The same operation in Neolithic Europe, thousands of years earlier.
Coca is often suggested, without proof, as the Andean surgeons' painkiller.

title: Coca: from Andean leaf to local anesthetic

confidence.note: Coca leaves and calcite from house floors in Peru's Nanchoc Valley are radiocarbon dated to at least 8,000 years ago; that is a minimum, and older finds could push it back. Niemann's isolation of cocaine and Koller's 1884 demonstration are well documented.

place: Nanchoc Valley, northern Peru; Göttingen; Vienna and Heidelberg
people: Albert Niemann, German chemist who isolated cocaine
summary: Andeans chewed coca 8,000 years ago; in 1884 its alkaloid, cocaine, let surgeons numb the human eye.
body: People in Peru's Nanchoc Valley were chewing coca by at least 8,000 years ago: leaves of that age lie in house floors beside pieces of calcite, which chewers use to draw the alkaloids out of the leaf. Albert Niemann isolated the main alkaloid, cocaine, in 1860. In September 1884 a paper by the young Viennese doctor Carl Koller, read for him at an ophthalmology congress in Heidelberg, showed that cocaine drops made the eye insensible to touch. News of local anesthesia spread around the world, and before the year was out some doctors experimenting with the drug had become addicted.

links.note: Coca is a suspected, unproven painkiller for Andean skull surgery.
General anesthesia arrived four decades before local anesthesia.

title: The Aztec herbal

confidence.note: The Latin manuscript survives and is dated 1552; its authors and its later travels through Spanish and Vatican libraries are well documented. Its Nahuatl original does not survive.

place: College of Santa Cruz, Tlatelolco (now Mexico City)
people: Martín de la Cruz, Nahua healer and author
Juan Badiano, Nahua lecturer at the college and Latin translator
summary: In 1552 two Nahua scholars produced a painted book of Mexican healing plants that spent four centuries in Europe.
body: In 1552, at the Franciscan College of Santa Cruz in Tlatelolco, a Nahua healer named Martín de la Cruz composed a book of Mexican healing plants in his own language, and Juan Badiano, a Nahua lecturer at the college, translated it into Latin. The *Libellus de medicinalibus Indorum herbis*, often called the Badianus Manuscript, has 185 paintings of plants and is the earliest known illustrated text of Nahua medicine. A friar commissioned it for Francisco de Mendoza, son of the viceroy of New Spain, and it may have been presented to the Emperor Charles V.

It then disappeared from view. It passed from the Spanish royal library to Cardinal Francesco Barberini and, in 1902, into the Vatican Library, where Charles Upson Clark found it in 1929. In 1990 Pope John Paul II returned it to Mexico; it is now kept by the National Institute of Anthropology and History. With Francisco Hernández's natural history of the 1570s and Bernardino de Sahagún's Florentine Codex of about 1577, it is one of three key sources on pre-Hispanic medicine, all of them made under Spanish rule.

links.note: The European herbal tradition whose format the Libellus echoed.
A near-contemporary Chinese compendium of healing plants.

title: The Great Dying

confidence.note: That epidemics killed a very large share of the Americas' Indigenous people in the century after 1492 is not in doubt. How many lived there beforehand, and so how many died, rests on sparse tribute records, censuses and archaeology, and estimates differ several-fold; the cause of the 1545 cocoliztli epidemic is also still argued.

place: The Caribbean, Mexico, the Andes and the wider Americas
summary: In the century after 1492, new diseases, war and enslavement killed perhaps nine in ten of the Americas' people.
body: In 1520 smallpox reached Mexico. By one estimate it killed 5 to 8 million people; another puts it at 30 to 50 percent of Mexico's Indigenous population. It was one wave among many. The first recorded outbreak after Columbus struck Hispaniola in 1497, smallpox spread into the Inca lands in the late 1520s, and influenza, measles, typhus and other infections followed, each hitting people who had never been exposed to them before.

How many died is fiercely debated, because nobody counted the Americas in 1492. Estimates of the population before contact have run from Dobyns's 112 million down to far lower figures, and loss rates from 40 to 95 percent. A 2019 synthesis of 119 regional estimates put the pre-contact population at about 60.5 million and the loss by 1600 at about 90 percent, some 55 million deaths. So much farmland went back to forest that it measurably lowered carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

Disease did not act alone. Warfare, enslavement and famine, as fields went untended by the sick, multiplied the toll. In New Spain, Indigenous laborers under the encomienda system were overworked and underfed, which likely left them more vulnerable.

Not every killer was obviously European. The *cocoliztli* (Nahuatl for "pest") of 1545 to 1548 killed an estimated 5 to 15 million people. Some researchers argued it was a native hemorrhagic fever carried by rodents during a megadrought. In 2018, DNA from victims buried at Teposcolula-Yucundaa in Oaxaca pointed instead to *Salmonella enterica* Paratyphi C, a cause of enteric fever: a strong candidate for that outbreak, though not proof of what caused the wider catastrophe.

myth.tradition: Native Americans died in such numbers because they were genetically too weak to resist European germs.
myth.record: Lack of prior exposure mattered, but there is no evidence that genetic differences made the diseases more deadly. Conquest itself, through war, slavery, forced labor and famine, made the epidemics far worse.

links.note: The other great demographic catastrophe, caused by a single pathogen.
Mexico City's colonial hospital opened as the epidemics began.
The disease that led the first wave was eradicated in 1980.

title: Hospital de Jesús, Mexico City

confidence.note: The founding by Cortés in 1524 is the standard date, though it rests on later institutional history rather than a surviving founding charter. It is generally called the oldest continuously operating hospital in the Americas, but other hospitals were working in the city at the same time.

people: Hernán Cortés, Spanish conqueror and founder
summary: Founded by Cortés in 1524, this Mexico City hospital still sees patients five centuries later.
body: Hernán Cortés founded a hospital in Mexico City in 1524, three years after his forces took the Aztec capital, on the spot where tradition says he first met Moctezuma in November 1519. First called the Hospital de la Purísima Concepción, it took its present name in 1665. Because Cortés created it as a secular foundation, it escaped the 19th-century Reform Laws that closed many church institutions. It still treats patients and is probably the oldest continuously operating hospital in the Americas.

links.note: Modeled on the charitable hospitals of Christian Europe.
It opened as epidemics devastated Mexico's Indigenous people.

title: Cinchona, the fever-bark

traditional.note: Legend says the Countess of Chinchón, cured of a fever in Peru, brought the bark to Spain in 1638.

confidence.note: Spanish use of the bark in Peru is documented from around 1630, but its early history was already a tangle of fact and legend when first compiled in 1663. How far Andean peoples used it before the Spanish is uncertain; the isolation of quinine in 1820 is firmly documented.

place: Peru and the Andes; Rome, London, Paris; later Java
people: Thomas Sydenham, English physician who came to champion the bark
Pierre Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Caventou, French chemists who isolated quinine
summary: A bitter Andean bark became Europe's one reliable fever cure, then quinine, a drug that helped carry empires into the tropics.
body: Around 1630, Spaniards in Peru began to record the use of a bitter tree bark against fever. Shipped to Europe by the Jesuit order, it became known as Jesuit's powder or *Cortex peruanus*, and through the later 17th century it was used ever more widely against intermittent fevers, the shaking agues that would be shown two centuries later to be malaria.

Where the knowledge began is unclear. The bark was not part of the Inca pharmacopeia, but Andean people appear to have used it against shivering. Europe preferred a romantic story, in which a Spanish countess was cured in Peru and carried the bark home. Even by 1663, when its history was first compiled, the bark's story was a mixture of fact and legend.

Its reception was fierce. Protestants distrusted a remedy promoted by Jesuits, and the market filled with weak or fake barks, since Europeans did not know the tree itself until botanists described it around 1730. Yet it won converts. Thomas Sydenham, lukewarm in 1666, a decade later called it "the only specific". In the 1690s, Jesuit missionaries in Beijing offered a pound of bark to the Kangxi Emperor, who had it tested on fever patients before taking it himself.

In 1820 the French chemists Pierre Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Caventou isolated quinine, making measured doses possible. Quinine then became a tool of empire. In West Africa, by one historian's estimate, half of newly arrived Europeans died within a year; British naval surgeons pressed for quinine as a preventive. After 1890 most quinine came from bark grown on Java rather than in South America. It remained a standard malaria treatment into the 21st century.

myth.tradition: The Countess of Chinchón, cured of fever in Peru, introduced the bark to Europe in 1638, and the tree is named after her.
myth.record: Linnaeus did name the tree *Cinchona* after her in 1742, but the cure story is legend. The documented trail begins with Spanish use in Peru around 1630 and Jesuit exports to Europe.

links.note: The cause of the fevers that quinine treated was found in the 1890s.
Another channel by which American plant knowledge reached Europe.

title: Onesimus and the Boston inoculations

confidence.note: The 1721 Boston epidemic and Boylston's inoculations are well documented, and his figures were published in 1726. What is known of Onesimus comes almost entirely from Cotton Mather, his enslaver.

people: Onesimus, enslaved African man in Cotton Mather's household
summary: An enslaved African man taught Boston's leading minister how to fight smallpox, and the numbers proved him right.
body: When smallpox struck Boston in 1721, the minister Cotton Mather already knew a way to blunt it, and he had learned it from Onesimus, an enslaved African man in his household. Onesimus described inoculation: deliberately giving a mild case of smallpox to protect against a severe one. By 1700 the practice had spread through Africa, India and the Ottoman Empire, and Mather had also read reports from Constantinople in the Royal Society's *Philosophical Transactions*.

With Mather's backing, the physician Zabdiel Boylston began inoculating, amid a furious public debate. He kept count. Of the 247 people he inoculated in 1721 and 1722, six died, about 2.4 percent. Of the 5,759 Bostonians who caught smallpox naturally, 844 died, roughly one in seven. Boylston published his figures in London in 1726. Among the earliest uses of numbers to judge a treatment, they helped inoculation win acceptance in England and its American colonies.

links.note: Inoculation reached London in the same year by another route.
The same practice recorded in India.
Inoculation paved the way for safer vaccination with cowpox.
